articles.text:
FHLBank Chicago: $62 Million Affordable Housing Grants To Support 1,786 Homes Across Illinois And Wisconsin
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:29 AM
FHLBank Chicago: $62 Million Affordable Housing Grants To Support 1,786 Homes Across Illinois And Wisconsin
The Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago has awarded $62 million through its 2026 Affordable Housing Program General Fund to finance 47 affordable housing projects in Illinois and Wisconsin. The funding will support the acquisition, rehabilitation, and construction of 1,786 affordable housing units across the two states.
The awards include an additional $10 million approved by FHLBank Chicago’s Board of Directors to expand support for affordable housing development.
The grants are intended to address housing affordability challenges as development costs and constrained housing supply continue to affect communities.
FHLBank Chicago operates as a regional member-owned cooperative within the Federal Home Loan Bank System.
Its member institutions include commercial banks, credit unions, insurance companies, savings institutions, and community development financial institutions.
The Affordable Housing Program provides grants to support projects sponsored through participating member institutions.
Applications are submitted by housing developers, government organizations, public housing authorities, tribally designated organizations, and other eligible participants.
The funding helps bridge gaps between the cost of providing affordable housing and the financing available through other sources.
The 2026 awards cover projects involving different housing needs and development approaches.
One recipient is Reclaiming Chicago NFP, which received support for the construction of 24 affordable single-family homes on vacant city-owned lots.
The homes will be developed across four Chicago neighborhoods: Back of the Yards, Roseland, North Lawndale, and Washington Park.
The project is sponsored by First Eagle Bank, a member of FHLBank Chicago.
It is part of an initiative organized by United Power for Action and Justice, a coalition that brings together civic and religious organizations.
Five nonprofit development partners are participating in the effort.
The project is intended to expand opportunities for homeownership while returning vacant properties to productive residential use.
First Eagle Bank has also provided a $1 million interest-free loan to support the development.
The combination of financing and grant support is intended to help move the project toward construction.
Another award will support Milwaukee Development Corporation’s conversion of a former hospital into affordable apartments.
The project will create 124 residences for adults ages 55 and older.
Of those units, 25 will be designated as supportive housing for residents with disabilities.
Jewish Family Services will provide on-site services to eligible residents.
Associated Bank is sponsoring the project through the Affordable Housing Program.
The redevelopment is intended to preserve a historic building while introducing additional affordable housing options for older adults.
Projects like these illustrate the program’s support for both new construction and the reuse of existing properties.
Since the Affordable Housing Program General Fund began in 1989, FHLBank Chicago has allocated more than $630 million in grants through the end of 2025.
These investments have helped provide housing for more than 85,000 households.

articles.text:
Oyster Therapeutics: $60 Million Series A-2 Funding To Advance Alzheimer’s Drug Development And Protein Degradation Platform
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 4:19 AM
Oyster Therapeutics: $60 Million Series A-2 Funding To Advance Alzheimer’s Drug Development And Protein Degradation Platform
Oyster Therapeutics, formerly known as Kesmalea Therapeutics, has raised $60 million in Series A-2 funding to advance its next-generation targeted protein degradation technology for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative conditions. The financing will support the development of the company’s lead oral tau degrader toward clinical trials while expanding its proprietary SELFTAC drug discovery platform. The round was led by 4BIO Capital, a London-based venture capital firm specializing in life sciences, with participation from new investors Eli Lilly and Company, CE Ventures, Actium Group, and TOHO Ventures, which is managed by Global Brain.
Existing investors Syncona, Oxford Science Enterprises, Mission BioCapital, and MGB Ventures also participated.
The financing comes as the company rebrands from Kesmalea Therapeutics to Oyster Therapeutics, reflecting its transition toward clinical development and broader ambitions in neuroscience.
Headquartered in London, Oyster is developing medicines based on targeted protein degradation, a therapeutic approach designed to eliminate disease-associated proteins by using the body’s natural cellular protein disposal mechanisms.
Unlike conventional treatments that may inhibit the activity of particular proteins, targeted protein degraders are designed to trigger their removal from cells.
Oyster is initially focusing on neurodegenerative diseases involving abnormal accumulations of the tau protein.
Tau plays an important role in maintaining healthy neuronal structures, but abnormal forms can accumulate and contribute to diseases known as tauopathies.
Alzheimer’s disease is among the best-known conditions associated with pathological tau accumulation.
The company’s lead program is an orally administered, brain-penetrant tau degrader designed to selectively remove harmful forms of tau while preserving healthy tau.
Developing medicines capable of reaching the central nervous system presents considerable challenges because the blood-brain barrier restricts the passage of many therapeutic compounds.
Traditional bifunctional protein degraders can be relatively large molecules, limiting their ability to cross biological membranes and reach brain tissue.
Oyster’s proprietary SELFTAC platform is designed to address this limitation by enabling larger targeted protein degraders to function as smaller molecular components.
The technology uses a reversible linker connecting two molecular structures, commonly called warheads.
One component binds to the targeted protein, while the other recruits the cellular machinery responsible for protein degradation.
The reversible linker enables the components to exist as smaller molecules that can more readily penetrate biological membranes.
The molecules are subsequently designed to self-assemble into a functional bifunctional degrader capable of triggering the removal of the intended protein.
Oyster believes this approach could improve central nervous system penetration while preserving the versatility of conventional targeted protein degradation technology.

articles.title: Bay: $50 Million Funding To Expand AI Agent Security Platform Across Enterprise Environments
articles.snippet:
Bay, an AI cybersecurity company developing technology to control autonomous agent activity, has emerged from stealth with $50 million in total funding. The financing includes a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures and a previously undisclosed $13 million seed round led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners. Additional Series A investors include Micron Ventures, M12, Microsoft's venture capital fund, and Assaf Rappaport, CEO of Wiz.
